post.title: Does Squad Value Decide World Cup Success?

tweets.text:
Five World Cups. 160 Squads. Billions on the Pitch.

Morocco were ranked 17th by squad value at the 2022 World Cup. They reached the semi-finals. Germany were ranked 6th. They went home in the group stage. So does the money matter? Across 160 squads...

Thread 🧵

160 squads, 5 World Cups, one chart. The pattern is real — richer squads cluster higher. But Germany 2018 (ranked 3rd) crashed out in the group stage. Morocco 2022 (ranked 17th) reached the semi-finals. So is this a correlation — or just noise?

It's a real pattern. Median squad value nearly doubles between group exits and semi-finalists — then doubles again for winners. Every winner since 2006 ranked in the top 7. 3 of those 5 won as the most expensive squad in the tournament.

The money cuts both ways. Spain 2014 and Germany 2018 arrived as top-5 squads — and went home in the group stage. Costa Rica 2014 and Morocco 2022 reached the knockouts as some of the cheapest squads in their tournament. The pattern works until it doesn't.

Costa Rica 2014: a quarter-final from the 4th-cheapest squad in the tournament. Morocco 2022: a semi-final, also from a low base. At the other end: Germany 2018 and Belgium 2022 — group stage exits from squads worth close to a billion euros.

England. Germany. Spain. Portugal. Belgium. The same names, every tournament, with the most expensive squads — and consistent underperformance. Belgium's Golden Generation won nothing. England haven't reached a World Cup final since 1966.

Croatia reached the 2018 final ranked 9th. The 2022 semi-finals ranked 12th. Japan, South Korea, and Morocco consistently punch above their squad value. In 2026 — the most expensive field ever — the overachievers will be the story again.
